# Introduction

Sorted L-One Penalized Estimation (SLOPE) [@bogdan2013; @zeng2014; @bogdan2015]
is a type of regularized regression that consists of solving the following
convex optimization problem:
$$
  \mathop{\mathrm{minimize}}_{\beta_0 \in \mathbb{R},\beta \in \mathbb{R}^p} \Big( P(\beta_0,\beta) = F(\beta_0, \beta) + \alpha J_\lambda(\beta) \Big)
$$ {#eq-slope}
where $P$ is the primal problem, $F$ is the loss function, $\alpha$ is a
parameter that controls the strength of regularization, and $\lambda$ is a
non-increasing sequence of penalty weights. $J$ is the *sorted $\ell_1$ norm*,
defined as
$$
  J_\lambda(\beta) = \sum_{j=1}^p \lambda_j |\beta_{(j)}|,
  \quad \text{where}\quad |\beta_{(1)}| \geq |\beta_{(2)}| \geq \ldots
                                        \geq |\beta_{(p)}|.
$$ {#eq-sorted-l1}

We will assume that $F$ takes the following form:
$$
  F( \beta_0, \beta )
  = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f( \beta_0 + x_i^\top \beta , y_i),
$$
where $f$ is a smooth, convex function and $x_i$ is the $i$th row of the
$n \times p$ design matrix $X$. Throughout the paper, we use scalar-response
notation and denote a row of $X$ by $x_i$ and a column by $x_j$. For multinomial
regression with $m$ classes, $y_i$ and $\beta_0$ instead have $m - 1$
components, $\beta$ is a $p \times (m - 1)$ matrix, and the sorted $\ell_1$ norm
acts on its vectorization. We let $(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta})$ denote a
solution to the problem in @eq-slope.

SLOPE is a generalization of both the
lasso[^1] [@santosa1986; @donoho1994; @donoho1995; @tibshirani1996] and
OSCAR[^2] (octagonal shrinkage and clustering algorithm for
regression) [@bondell2008]. One of the most important properties of SLOPE is
that it can cluster coefficients by setting them to the same
magnitude [@figueiredo2016; @hejny2025; @bogdan2026]. This is a natural
consequence of the sorted $\ell_1$ norm, stemming from the fact that the
contribution to the norm of a given coefficient increases disproportionately if
it changes order. This also allows SLOPE to better recover the ordering pattern
in the solution.

Like the lasso, SLOPE is a convex but non-smooth optimization problem. And since
the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm (PAVA) [@barlow1972] can be used to
efficiently[^3] compute the proximal operator of the sorted $\ell_1$ norm, it is
possible to use a wide range of proximal algorithms, such as proximal gradient
descent, to solve SLOPE. This also includes accelerated methods such as
FISTA [@beck2009], which was for instance used by @bogdan2015. Other
possibilities include proximal Newton [@lee2014] and the alternating direction
method of multipliers (ADMM) method [@boyd2010].

For similar problems such as the lasso and elastic net [@zou2005], however,
these aforementioned methods have generally found themselves outperformed by
coordinate descent methods [@friedman2007; @friedman2010], which optimize one
coefficient at a time. Several efficient implementations of coordinate descent
algorithms exists for the lasso, elastic net, and other $\ell_1$-based
regularization methods. For R, there is for instance **glmnet** [@friedman2010],
which fits generalized linear models, including Cox-proportional hazards models,
with elastic net regularization. Other notable packages are
**ncvreg** [@breheny2011], which in addition to the elastic net also supports
non-convex penalties such as SCAD [@fan2001] and MCP [@zhang2010]. Another
interesting package is **biglasso** [@zeng2021], which supports out-of-memory
data to fit lasso models to large datasets. Finally, there is also
**lars** [@efron2004], which fits exact lasso solution paths using the least
angle regression (LARS) algorithm. For Python, there is support for the elastic
net in the widely used **scikit-learn** [@pedregosa2011] module, which beyond
the coordinate descent algorithm also features LARS and alternative solvers for
the lasso and elastic net. For Julia, there is generally less support for
regularized regression. There exists a wrapper for **glmnet** in
**GLMNet.jl** [@kornblith2024a] and a native Julia package in
**Lasso.jl** [@kornblith2024].

Unfortunately, coordinate descent requires that the objective is separable in
$(\beta_0, \beta)$, which is not the case in SLOPE due to the permutations
involved in the sorted $\ell_1$ norm, which means that coordinate descent cannot
be used directly. This problem was, however, overcome by @larsson2023, who
invented a hybrid combination of proximal gradient and coordinate descent. The
algorithm alternates between proximal gradient descent steps on the full problem
and coordinate descent on a collapsed problem corresponding to the current
cluster structure, to achieve robust and fast convergence.

In this paper we make this algorithm available to a wide audience by presenting
a collection of packages in R [@rcoreteam2025],
Python [@pythonsoftwarefoundation2025], Julia [@bezanson2017], and C++. For
Julia, our package is, to the best of our knowledge, the first and only
available implementation of SLOPE. For Python, **tick** [@bacry2018] provides a
SLOPE proximal operator that can be combined with its solvers, and
**skglm** [@moufad2025] supports fitting SLOPE with FISTA. Our **sortedl1**
package makes the hybrid coordinate descent algorithm described above available
in Python. For R, our package was the first implementation of SLOPE, although
there is now also support through the **sgs** [@feser2023] and
**grpSLOPE** [@brzyski2018] packages. Additionally, an implementation for MATLAB
is also available from @candes2013 and is also included in TFOCS [@becker2011].

## Outline of the paper

In @sec-math-details, we introduce the statistical problem that our packages
solve, namely generalized linear models (GLMs) regularized with the sorted
$\ell_1$ norm (SLOPE)[^4], and provide a brief overview of the mathematical
properties of GLMs and the particular properties of SLOPE. We discuss the
optimization problem and describe the hybrid coordinate descent algorithm we use
for solving SLOPE. In @sec-implementation-details, we provide a detailed
overview of the software implementations, highlighting technical aspects such as
memory management, parallelization, and convergence criteria. In @sec-examples,
we showcase how our packages work in practice, providing examples of fitting
models, plotting, and performing cross-validation. Finally, in @sec-discussion,
we summarize the contributions of this paper and discuss future work.

# Mathematical details {#sec-math-details}

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the mathematical details of the
SLOPE optimization problem, including the objective and the hybrid coordinate
descent algorithm used to solve it. We also discuss the convergence criteria
used to determine when the algorithm has converged, and the path fitting
procedure used to compute the full regularization path for SLOPE.

## Generalized linear models

Our packages are designed to solve SLOPE for generalized linear models (GLMs),
in which the response $y_i$ is modeled as a random variable from an exponential
family, and is assumed to depend conditionally on the linear predictor
$\eta_i = x_i^\top \beta + \beta_0$ via
$\mathbb{E}(y_i \mid \eta_i) = g^{-1}(\eta_i)$, where $g^{-1}$ is the inverse
link function. This gives rise to the following form of the loss function:
$$
  F( \beta_0, \beta ) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f( \eta_i, y_i),
$$
where $f$ is the contribution of the $i$th observation to the negative
log-likelihood of the model. To estimate the parameters of a generalized linear
model, $(\beta_0, \beta)$, we minimize the loss function $F$ with respect to
$(\beta_0, \beta)$.

A special property of $f$ is that its partial derivative with respect to $\eta$
is
$$
  \frac{\partial}{\partial \eta_i} f( \eta_i, y_i) = g^{-1}( \eta_i) - y_i
                                                   = r_i,
$$
where we define $r_i$ to be the *generalized residual*. As a consequence, the
gradient of the loss function with respect to $\beta$ can be expressed as
$$
  \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_j} F( \beta_0, \beta )
  = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} \frac{\partial}{\partial \eta_i} f( \eta_i, y_i)
  = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} r_i.
$$

We summarize the loss, link, and inverse link functions for the GLMs supported
by the SLOPE packages in @tbl-glm.

  | Model       | Loss                                                                              | Link                                                 | Inverse link                                                                    |
  | :--         | :--                                                                               | :--                                                  | :--                                                                             |
  | Gaussian    | $\frac{1}{2}(y - \eta)^2$                                                         | $\mu$                                                | $\eta$                                                                          |
  | Binomial    | $\log(1 + e^\eta) - \eta y$                                                       | $\log\left( \frac{\mu}{1 - \mu} \right)$             | $\frac{e^\eta}{1 + e^\eta}$                                                     |
  | Poisson     | $e^\eta - \eta y$                                                                 | $\log(\mu)$                                          | $e^\eta$                                                                        |
  | Multinomial | $\log\left( 1 + \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} e^{\eta_j} \right) - \sum_{k=1}^{m-1} y_k\eta_k$ | $\left( \log\frac{\mu_k}{\mu_m} \right)_{k=1}^{m-1}$ | $\left( \frac{e^{\eta_k}}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} e^{\eta_j}} \right)_{k=1}^{m-1}$ |

  : Loss functions, link functions, and inverse link functions for generalized
    linear models in the SLOPE package. For multinomial logistic regression, the
    input is vector-valued and $\mu_m = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{m-1}\mu_k$ is the mean
    of the reference class. {#tbl-glm}

A particular case of interest is the multinomial logistic regression model. Many
implementations of regularized multinomial logistic regression models, such as
those by @friedman2010 and @fercoq2015, use the *redundant* $m$-class
formulation. Here, however, we have opted to use the non-redundant formulation
of the loss function, with the last class serving as the reference category.
This choice slightly complicates the notation and leads to a more complex
formulation for the dual problem. For SLOPE, however, this is a more natural
choice, since it generalizes to the binary case as well (in which the last class
is also implicit).[^5] Furthermore, it also relieves the problem of the
parameter ambiguity that affects the redundant formulation, where rows of the
coefficient matrix can be shifted without changing the value of
$F(\beta_0, \beta)$. This also means that the redundant formulation needs to be
accompanied by a bounds adjustment step [@friedman2010]. This is trivial in the
case of the lasso and ridge, and only slightly more complicated for the elastic
net. For SLOPE, however, the situation is much more involved since rows of the
coefficient matrix cannot be arbitrarily shifted, since this could affect the
entire clustering structure.

## Hybrid algorithm

The primary algorithm of the **SLOPE** packages is the hybrid coordinate descent
algorithm by @larsson2023. Since it is described in detail there, we will only
summarize its key points here and highlight some of the improvements that we
have made to the original algorithm. The basic idea is to perform the coordinate
descent updates on the clusters' coefficients rather than directly on the
coefficients.

For a fixed $\beta$ such that $|\beta_j|$ takes $m$ distinct values, we let
$\mathcal{C}_1, \mathcal{C}_2 , \dots, \mathcal{C}_m$ and $c_1, c_2, \dots, c_m$
be the indices and coefficients, respectively, of the $m$ clusters of $\beta$,
such that $\mathcal{C}_i = \{j : |\beta_j| = c_i\}$ and
$c_1 > c_2 > \cdots > c_m \geq 0.$

In our algorithm, we fix the current cluster, e.g. $\mathcal{C}_k$, and update
all coefficients belonging to it in a single step. By itself, this algorithm is
not guaranteed to converge, since it can only reorder or merge clusters. To
circumvent this, the algorithm must be combined with proximal gradient descent
steps. These steps are able to split the clusters, which eventually means that
the full algorithm converges to the correct clusters and global minimum.

We have outlined the algorithm in @algo-hybrid. Unlike the implementation in
@larsson2023, this algorithm is extended to any generalized linear model---not
just the Gaussian case. To do so, we use an iteratively reweighted least-squares
(IRLS) approach, determining weights $w$ and a working response $z$ after each
proximal gradient descent step. We then run the coordinate descent algorithm for
a fixed number of iterations. Convergence is monitored using a duality-based
stopping criterion (@sec-convergence-criteria-details), which we check after
each gradient computation. To avoid complicating the presentation, we have
omitted some details of the algorithm here.

```pseudocode
#| label: algo-hybrid
#| html-comment-delimiter: "//"
#| html-line-number: true
#| html-no-end: false
#| pdf-placement: "ht"
#| pdf-line-number: true

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Hybrid coordinate descent for generalized linear models.}
\begin{algorithmic}
\State \textit{Input:} $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$, $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $\lambda_1\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_p>0$, maximum coordinate passes $v$
\Repeat
    \State Set $t$ by backtracking line search
    \State $\beta \gets \operatorname{prox}_{t\alpha J_\lambda}\bigl(\beta-t\nabla_\beta F(\beta_0,\beta)\bigr)$
    \For{$i\gets 1,\ldots,n$}
        \State $\eta_i\gets x_i^\top\beta+\beta_0$
        \State $w_i\gets \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\eta_i^2}f(\eta_i,y_i)$ \Comment{IRLS weights}
        \State $z_i\gets\eta_i-r_i(\eta_i,y_i)/w_i$ \Comment{IRLS working response}
    \EndFor
    \State Update $c$ and $\mathcal{C}$
    \For{$\mathrm{it}\gets 1,\ldots,v$}
        \State $k\gets 1$; $\beta^{\mathrm{old}}\gets\beta$
        \While{$k\leq |\mathcal{C}|$}
            \State $\tilde{x}\gets\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_k}x_j\operatorname{sign}(\beta_j)$
            \State $\tilde{r}\gets X\beta+\beta_0-z$ \Comment{Residuals}
            \State $\gamma\gets\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\tilde{x}_i\tilde{r}_i$ \Comment{Gradient}
            \State $\xi\gets\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\tilde{x}_i^2$ \Comment{Hessian}
            \State $\tilde{c}\gets T(c_k\xi-\gamma;\xi,c^{\setminus k},\lambda)$
            \State $\beta_{\mathcal{C}_k}\gets\tilde{c}\operatorname{sign}(\beta_{\mathcal{C}_k})$
            \State Update $c$ and $\mathcal{C}$
            \State $k\gets k+1$
        \EndWhile
        \If{$P(\beta)\geq P(\beta^{\mathrm{old}})$}
            \State $\beta\gets\beta^{\mathrm{old}}$
            \State \textbf{break}
        \EndIf
    \EndFor
\Until{$P(\beta_0,\beta)-D(\delta)\leq\varepsilon|P(\beta_0,\beta)|$}
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

The algorithm uses IRLS weights $w$ and a working response $z$ computed after
each proximal gradient step. We show the cyclical version and omit the intercept
updates for simplicity. The vector $c^{\setminus k}$ is $c$ with coefficient $k$
omitted, and $T$ is the SLOPE thresholding operator illustrated in
@fig-slope-thresholding.

```{r}
#| label: fig-slope-thresholding
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   An illustration of the SLOPE thresholding operator for $\beta = [0.5, -
#|   0.5, 0.3, 0.7]^\top$, and thus $c = \{0.7, 0.5, 0.3\}$, where we consider
#|   an update for the second cluster, $C_2 = \{1, 2\}$. We have omitted the
#|   particular value of $\omega$ for brevity. The example is adapted from
#|   @larsson2023. Across regions where the function is constant, the operator
#|   sets the result to be either exactly 0 or merges the cluster with another
#|   cluster, setting their magnitudes to be equal.
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("slope-thresholding"))
```

The hybrid nature of the algorithm is not only useful for enabling the
coordinate descent steps, but also comes with benefits due to the inclusion of
the PGD steps. Proximal gradient descent algorithms are known to converge under
more general assumptions than coordinate descent algorithms [@wright2015], which
means that the PGD part of the algorithm can serve as a fallback in case the
coordinate descent part does not converge. In practice, we store the current
solution before updating and revert to the previous solution if the coordinate
descent step does not improve the primal objective.

The implementation in @larsson2023 used a type of cyclical coordinate descent in
which the algorithm iterated over the clusters in descending order by their
coefficients' magnitudes. Although simple to implement and efficient for many
problems, cyclical coordinate descent is known to suffer from convergence issues
in some cases [@wright2015], which we found to be the case for SLOPE as well.
For the current implementation, we therefore include, and default to, a version
using random permutations, which is slightly slower but more robust.

## Convergence criteria

Our packages use a duality-based stopping criterion, providing an upper bound on
suboptimality at convergence. We transform the primal problem,
$P(\beta_0, \beta)$, into a constrained formulation and derive a dual problem,
$D(\delta)$, that allows us to compute a duality gap. As a stopping criterion,
we use the relative duality gap:
$$
  P( \beta_0, \beta ) - D( \delta ) \leq \varepsilon | P( \beta_0, \beta ) |,
$$
where $\varepsilon > 0$ is the user-defined tolerance level. This provides a
reliable, solver-independent measure of convergence. The complete derivation of
the dual problem and the calculation of the duality gap is provided in
@sec-convergence-criteria-details.

## Path fitting

Since optimal settings of $\alpha$ are only available under strict assumptions
that are typically hard to test, it is common to instead use cross-validation to
tune $\alpha$ over a grid of values. In practice, this means that we repeatedly
have to fit the full regularization path, which is the sequence of solutions to
the problem in @eq-slope as $\alpha$ is varied from $\alpha_\text{max}$ (the
value at which the first cluster enters the model) to a small value of $\alpha$
at which the model is almost saturated. Our packages are optimized to
efficiently compute the full regularization path, and make use of screening
rules (@sec-screening-rules) to speed up the process of doing so.

We use the same criteria as @friedman2010 for stopping the path early, except
that we stop if the number of *clusters*, excluding the zero-cluster, exceeds
$n + 1$ (by default), since the support of SLOPE is limited at $n$ clusters[^6].
This can potentially exceed the number of non-zero coefficients, although in
practice this is rare since clusters do not form easily at low levels of
regularization.

## Screening rules {#sec-screening-rules}

Sparse models like lasso and SLOPE are well-known to benefit from *screening
rules*, which are used to reduce the dimension of $\beta$ for a fixed $\lambda$
in the optimization problem and thereby speed up optimization. The intuition for
this is that it is possible to estimate the gradient $\nabla F(\beta)$ for a
given SLOPE problem and, via the subdifferential, estimate the support of the
solution: the identity of the nonzero coefficients. Screening rules are either
*heuristic* or *safe*. In the latter case the rule guarantees that excluded
predictors correspond to zero coefficients in the final model. Heuristic rules,
on the other hand, do not guarantee this and therefore need to be complemented
with a pass over all coefficients at the end to ensure that the optimality
conditions are satisfied. But since heuristic rules are typically less
conservative, the computational gains often outweigh this extra cost in
practice.

In the SLOPE package, we use the strong screening rule for
SLOPE [@larsson2020a], which is an extension of the working set strategy for the
strong screening rule for the lasso [@tibshirani2012].

# Implementation details {#sec-implementation-details}

In this section, we provide an overview of the implementation details of the
SLOPE packages, including the data structures used to represent clusters, the
thresholding operator, and parallelization strategies.

## Software architecture

We have implemented a collection of packages for solving SLOPE, currently with
support for R, Python, and Julia. The backbone of all of these packages is based
on a C++ library that implements all of the numerical algorithms for SLOPE,
including preprocessing, cross-validation, and path fitting. The packages for
the high-level languages all serve as thin wrappers to the C++ library, with
some additional functionality for handling data and plotting the results. This
means that new features and bug fixes propagate quickly and easily to all these
wrappers and enable users to promptly take advantage of the latest developments.
The entire suite of packages is open source and available in version-controlled
online repositories (@tbl-slope-packages).

  | Language | Package      | Repository                                                       | Documentation                                                  |
  | :--      | :--          | :--                                                              | :--                                                            |
  | R        | **SLOPE**    | [github.com/jolars/SLOPE](https://github.com/jolars/SLOPE)       | [jolars.github.io/SLOPE](https://jolars.github.io/SLOPE)       |
  | Python   | **sortedl1** | [github.com/jolars/sortedl1](https://github.com/jolars/sortedl1) | [jolars.github.io/sortedl1](https://jolars.github.io/sortedl1) |
  | Julia    | **SLOPE.jl** | [github.com/jolars/SLOPE.jl](https://github.com/jolars/SLOPE.jl) | [jolars.github.io/SLOPE.jl](https://jolars.github.io/SLOPE.jl) |
  | C++      | **slope**    | [github.com/jolars/libslope](https://github.com/jolars/libslope) | [jolars.github.io/libslope](https://jolars.github.io/libslope) |

  : The packages for solving SLOPE, with links to their source code repositories
    and documentation. {#tbl-slope-packages}

This is made possible via several pieces of software that enable us to link the
API from our C++ library to the high-level languages. This includes
**Rcpp** [@eddelbuettel2011] and **RcppEigen** [@bates2013] for R,
**pybind11** [@jakob2025], and **CxxWrap** [@janssens2020] for Julia.

## Core algorithmic components

Handling the cluster structure of SLOPE is a key part of the algorithm since we
will both be iterating over the clusters as part of the coordinate descent
updates as well as updating the clusters after each update. In our
implementation, we represent the clusters as a collection of three vectors:

`c`

:   The coefficients of the clusters

`c_idx`

:   Pointers to the coefficients in the cluster

`c_ptr`

:   Values of the cluster pointers

In this representation, the indices for the $k$th cluster are given by

```text
c_idx[c_ptr[k] : c_ptr[k+1]]
```

and the coefficient is simply `c[k]`. This structure is the same basic setup as
in @larsson2023. Unlike their implementation, however, we have made improvements
to the handling of updating the clusters (merging, reordering, removal), which
can now be performed with negligible overhead and with minimal copying.

The SLOPE thresholding operator (@fig-slope-thresholding) is the analogue to the
soft-thresholding operator for the lasso. But unlike the latter, which is
trivial to compute, the SLOPE thresholding operator needs to conduct a search
over the clusters in order to find correct solution. This leads to a worst-case
complexity that depends on the number of clusters, which might seem to be
prohibitive when both $n$ and $p$ are large. Fortunately, however, the situation
is much less dire in practice, since the order of the clusters typically
stabilizes early during optimization. In benchmarks, we have found that it makes
no difference whether we use a linear search or a binary search for real data
sets, and we have therefore opted for the simpler linear search. Note also that
the partial $\lambda$ sums do not need to be computed directly. Instead, we
simply compute the cumulative sum of the $\lambda$ array once and use this to
retrieve the partial sums as needed.

## Data handling and optimization

Our package is based on the **Eigen** C++ library and provides support for both
dense and sparse design matrices. The latter can be constructed through the
**Matrix** (R), **scipy** (Python), and **SparseArrays** (Julia) packages and
are passed to the C++ API without copying and with negligible overhead.
Coefficients are returned in a sparse format, which allows for efficient storage
and retrieval of the coefficients.

For dense matrices, the packages implement memory-efficient views of the input
matrices to avoid copying the data. This means, for instance, that no copies
need to be made when separating data sets into training and test data. Due to
this memory-efficient implementation, we provide an option to altogether avoid
copying the data during cross-validation. This allows us to parallelize the
cross-validation procedure over arbitrarily many folds and repetitions without
needing to ever copy the data, which makes for a much more memory-friendly
implementation (at the cost of worse runtime performance).

The SLOPE packages also support out-of-memory storage for the design matrix,
which means that users can fit SLOPE models on data sets that are larger than
the available memory. Storage in RAM is therefore limited to the order of
$O(n) + O(p)$, which means that the packages can be used on huge data sets. This
is supported via the generic `Eigen::Map` class, which allows arbitrary data to
be mapped into **Eigen** data structures. At the time of writing, this is only
supported for R, which is possible via the **bigmemory** package [@kane2013],
and currently only for dense designs.

As shown by @larsson2025, predictor normalization (centering and scaling the
design matrix) may have large consequences for the solutions. Our packages
provide multiple different options for centering and scaling, independently of
one another. We also provide the possibility to manually supply centering and
scaling vectors. Optionally, normalization is also realized just-in-time (JIT),
which means that the design matrix does not need to be normalized in place.
Normalization is performed as predictors of the design matrix are accessed
during optimization, which allows us to support centering even of sparse design
matrices. This also allows us to completely avoid copying the design matrix.

The software is parallelized using **OpenMP**, which is supported on all major
platforms. Our functions employ several heuristics based on problem size to
determine whether to spawn multiple threads, except for the case of
cross-validation, which is always parallelized.

# Examples {#sec-examples}

The packages are available through the respective package managers for each
language and can be installed using the following commands:

- R: `install.packages("SLOPE")`
- Python: `pip install sortedl1`
- Julia: `using Pkg; Pkg.add("SLOPE")`

Installing the C++ library is slightly more involved, and requires **CMake**
[@kitware2025] together with a working C++ toolchain, including the **Eigen**
library [@guennebaud2010a] and **OpenMP** [@dagum1998] (optionally, to enable
parallelization).

Assuming we have loaded a data set consisting of a design matrix `x` and
response vector `y`, we can fit the full regularization path for the SLOPE model
using the following commands in the different languages:

**R**

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

library(SLOPE)
fit <- SLOPE(x, y)
```

**Python**

```python
import sortedl1

model = sortedl1.Slope()
fit = model.path(x, y)
```

**Julia**

```julia
using SLOPE
fit = slope(x, y)
```

You can also use the C++ library directly, in which case the above would
translate into the following:

```cpp
#include <slope.h>
slope::Slope model;
auto path_result = model.path(x, y);
```

In the sequel, we will focus our examples on the R package, but please see
@sec-examples-julia-python for equivalent examples in Python, Julia, and C++.

## First steps {#sec-first-steps}

We start with a simple example of fitting a full SLOPE path to the diabetes data
set [@efron2004], including plotting it.[^7]

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

library(SLOPE)
data("diabetes", package = "lars")
x <- scale(diabetes$x)
y <- diabetes$y
fit_slope <- SLOPE(x, y, q = 0.4)
plot(fit_slope)
```

The `q` parameter is a parameter of the sequence of $\lambda$ values, which by
default (`lambda = "bh"`) uses the Benjamini--Hochberg (BH)
sequence [@bogdan2015]. If the design matrix is orthogonal, then the `q`
parameter sets a desired false discovery rate (FDR) in terms of the
identification of true signals (nonzero coefficients).

Other types of sequences are also supported, including `lambda = "lasso"` for
the lasso, `lambda = "oscar"` for the OSCAR sequence [@bondell2008], and
`lambda = "gaussian"` for the Gaussian-type sequence [@bogdan2015], which is a
modification of the BH sequence that has been empirically shown to provide
similar FDR control in non-orthogonal, low-dimensional settings.

To show how the choice of the $\lambda$ sequence affects the results, we will
refit the diabetes data using the lasso sequence.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

fit_lasso <- SLOPE(x, y, lambda = "lasso")
plot(fit_lasso)
```

The resulting paths are plotted in @fig-diabetes. Observe that the paths are
similar but that SLOPE has clustered some coefficients along parts of the path.
Predictors 3 and 9, for instance, enter the path together and remain clustered
at the beginning, then split apart and again cluster together briefly, before
diverging again. We also see that predictors 4, 10, and 8 enter the model
together, only to then, one by one, split apart later on. Unlike the lasso path,
there are many more *kinks* in the SLOPE path, since they occur not only when
new predictors become active, but also when they merge into or split from
clusters.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diabetes
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   SLOPE and lasso paths on the diabetes data set. Note that the $x$ axis is
#|   reversed. Numbers indicate the indices of the predictors.
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("diabetes-slope-lasso"))
```

## Relaxed SLOPE

To attain sparsity, SLOPE shrinks coefficients towards zero. This introduces
bias, which, although it helps to combat overfitting, may also lead to worse
predictions in some cases. To mitigate this, it is possible to *relax* the SLOPE
solutions by fitting an ordinary least-squares model to the collapsed cluster
structure from running SLOPE [@skalski2022][^8]. The level of relaxation is
parameterized by $\gamma$, which controls the mix between the original SLOPE
solution ($\gamma = 1$) and the fully relaxed solution ($\gamma = 0$), so that
the end result is given by
$$
  \hat{\beta} = \gamma \hat{\beta}_\text{SLOPE}
                + (1 - \gamma ) \hat{\beta}_\text{relaxed} .
$$

Our packages support relaxation through the `gamma` argument. Here, we fit fully
relaxed ($\gamma = 0$) and semi-relaxed ($\gamma = 0.5$) models, along with
standard SLOPE ($\gamma = 1$) for comparison.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

fit_relaxed <- SLOPE(x, y, q = 0.1, gamma = 0)
fit_semirelaxed <- SLOPE(x, y, q = 0.1, gamma = 0.5)
fit_standard <- SLOPE(x, y, q = 0.1, gamma = 1)
```

We plot the resulting paths in @fig-relaxed-slope. Observe the jaggedness of the
relaxed paths, which change dramatically as clusters form, merge, and split.

```{r}
#| label: fig-relaxed-slope
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   SLOPE with various levels of relaxation $\gamma$, with $\gamma = 0$ (fully
#|   relaxed), $\gamma = 0.5$ (semi-relaxed), and $\gamma = 1$ (standard SLOPE).
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("slope-relaxed"))
```

## Cross-validation

Our packages support hyper-parameter tuning via iterated $k$-fold
cross-validation (CV), with parameterization over $\alpha$, $\lambda$ type (BH,
Gaussian type, etc.), $\gamma$ (SLOPE relaxation parameter). Here, we
demonstrate the CV functionality by cross-validating across two values of the
$q$ parameter and printing the results, which displays the optimal values for
all the cross-validated parameters.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

set.seed(48)
fit_cv <- cvSLOPE(x, y, q = c(0.1, 0.2))
fit_cv
```
```{r}
#| label: output-diabetes-cv
#| echo: false

cat(paper_results$diabetes$cv_text, sep = "\n")
```

It is also easy to plot the cross-validation results (@fig-cv), which show the
cross-validation error with 95% confidence intervals and a dashed line
indicating the optimal value of $\alpha$ for the best value of $q$.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

plot(fit_cv)
```
```{r}
#| label: fig-cv
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Mean-squared error (MSE) from cross-validation of $q$ and $\alpha$ for
#|   SLOPE fit to the diabetes data set. The dashed line marks the optimal value
#|   of $\alpha$ in the panel corresponding to the optimal value of $q$.
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("slope-cv"))
```

# Benchmarks

In this section, we present benchmarks of the numerical performance of our
implementation for solving SLOPE. In @sec-single-solution-benchmark, we examine
the performance of SLOPE when fitting for a single value of $\alpha$, while in
@sec-path-benchmark, we benchmark the performance of fitting the full
regularization path.

Our benchmarks are organized and run using **benchopt** [@moreau2022a]. They are
available as public git repositories at
[`github.com/benchopt/benchmark_slope`](https://github.com/benchopt/benchmark_slope)
and
[`github.com/jolars/benchmark_slope_path`](https://github.com/jolars/benchmark_slope_path)
for the single solution and path benchmarks, respectively. Both feature the
Python version of our implementation, **sortedl1**[^9]. The single solution
benchmark includes four variations on proximal gradient descent (PGD), using
Anderson acceleration [@anderson1965; @zhang2020], Barzilai--Borwein step sizes,
safe screening rules, and the fast iterative shrinking and thresholding
algorithm (FISTA) [@beck2009]. The latter of these is also included through the
**skglm** package [@bertrand2022] and the **tick** package [@bacry2018]. We also
include the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) [@boyd2010], a
semi-smooth Newton-based method [@luo2019], and an approximate homotopy method,
**SolutionPath** [@dupuis2024]. See @sec-solver-details for more details on the
solvers and their implementations. The path benchmark compares **sortedl1** with
a subset of these solvers, namely **FISTA**, **SolutionPath**, and **ADMM**. All
of the benchmarks were run on a system with an AMD Ryzen 9 7900 CPU (12 cores
and 24 threads, with a maximum boost clock of 5.5 GHz), 64 GB of RAM, and NixOS
26.11 (Linux).

We have run the benchmarks for both simulated (@tbl-simulated-data) as well as
real data (@tbl-real-data). For all real data, we standardize the predictors to
have mean zero and unit variance if $X$ is dense and scale with the maximum
absolute value of each predictor otherwise. For all data we use the
Benjamini--Hochberg sequence for $\lambda$ with $q = 0.2$. Since some of the
solvers cannot handle intercepts, we have omitted the intercepts from the
models. Also note that not all solvers support sparse design matrices, which is
why they are not included everywhere.

We evaluate convergence using a solver-independent relative duality gap and stop
sampling each convergence curve once this measure reaches $10^{-7}$. For
solution paths, we apply the same target to the maximum relative duality gap
along the path. Values below this threshold are not distinguished in the
figures. The solvers retain their native internal stopping rules, so the common
duality-gap measure, rather than an internal tolerance parameter, provides the
basis for comparison. We use Benchopt's 30-second timeout, which is checked
between successive evaluations of a solver, and restrict the figures to
evaluations taking no more than 30 seconds.

  | Dataset | $n$ | $p$ | $X$ density | References |
  | :-- | --: | --: | --: | :-- |
  | `BRCA1` | 536 | 17,322 | 1 | @nationalcancerinstitute2022 |
  | `Koussounadis2014` | 101 | 34,694 | 1 | @koussounadis2014 |
  | `Real-Sim` | 72,309 | 20,958 | 0.0025 | @mccallum2010 |
  | `RCV1` | 20,242 | 44,504 | 0.0017 | @lewis2004 |
  | `Rhee2006` | 842 | 360 | 0.025 | @rhee2006 |
  | `YearPredictionMSD` | 463,715 | 90 | 1 | @bertin-mahieux2011 |

  : Real datasets used in our experiments, with numbers of samples $n$ and
    predictors $p$. `BRCA1`, `Koussounadis2014`, and `Rhee2006` were obtained
    from @breheny2022, and the remaining datasets from @chang2016. Densities are
    rounded to two significant figures. {#tbl-real-data}

  | Scenario         | $n$    | $p$     | $s$ | $X$ density | $\rho$ |
  | :--------------- | -----: | ------: | --: | ----------: | -----: |
  | High Dim         |    100 |  20,000 |  20 |           1 |    0.6 |
  | High Dim, Sparse |  2,000 | 200,000 |  20 |       0.001 |    0.6 |
  | Low Dim          | 20,000 |     100 |  40 |           1 |    0.6 |

  : Simulated benchmark scenarios. $\rho$ is the autocorrelation between
    adjacent predictors, $s$ is the number of nonzero true coefficients, and $n$
    and $p$ are the numbers of samples and predictors. {#tbl-simulated-data}

## Single solution {#sec-single-solution-benchmark}

We have parameterized our single-solution benchmarks by $\alpha$ as a fraction
of $\alpha_\text{max}$ (the value at which the first cluster enters the model),
and run the benchmarks for $\alpha = \alpha_\text{max} / 2$,
$\alpha_\text{max} / 10$, and $\alpha_\text{max} / 50$. We present convergence
using the duality gap.

The results for the simulated data are presented in @fig-simulated-data-single.
At the displayed relative-duality-gap threshold of $10^{-7}$, our algorithm is
the first to reach the threshold in all nine combinations of simulation setting
and regularization level. The difference is especially pronounced for high
levels of regularization, where our method is often many times faster than the
next best method. Newt-ALM also reaches the threshold rapidly in the
($\alpha_\text{max} / 50$, High Dim) setting, although **sortedl1** reaches it
first. Our current implementation shows improved performance compared to
@larsson2023, which also featured the hybrid method. We believe this is likely
due to the addition of screening rules as well as algorithmic improvements.
Newt-ALM also performs better than in @larsson2023, following improvements to
the implementation used here.

```{r}
#| label: fig-simulated-data-single
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Performance of the solvers for the single solution benchmark for three different settings of simulated data\u00a0(@tbl-simulated-data). Please see the text for information about the data and setup of the experiment."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("benchmark_single_simulated"))
```

For real data @fig-real-data-single, we see a mostly similar pattern. At a
relative duality gap of $10^{-7}$, **sortedl1** is the first solver to reach the
threshold in 15 of the 18 combinations. Newt-ALM is first for `Koussounadis2014`
at $\alpha_\text{max}/50$, and ADMM is first for `YearPredictionMSD` at
$\alpha_\text{max}/10$ and $\alpha_\text{max}/50$. The performance of the other
algorithms is generally more sensitive to the dataset and regularization level.

```{r}
#| label: fig-real-data-single
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Performance of the solvers for the single solution benchmark for six different real data sets\u00a0(@tbl-real-data) and three levels of regularization. Please see the text for information about the data and setup of the experiment."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("benchmark_single_real"))
```

## Path {#sec-path-benchmark}

Here, we present benchmarks on a subset of the real data sets from
@tbl-real-data. We parameterize the benchmark using the length of the path,
using 50, 100, and 200 steps. We present the results as the maximum relative
duality gap along the path.

The results are presented in @fig-real-data-path. Note that the interpretation
of progress towards convergence does not hold quite the same way as for the
single solution benchmarks since we fit a full path. Nevertheless, **sortedl1**
is the only solver to reduce the maximum relative duality gap to $10^{-7}$,
reaching it in eight of the nine combinations of dataset and path length, and
doing so by a large time margin. No solver reaches the threshold for `BRCA1`
with 200 path points within the time limit; **sortedl1** comes closest, with a
maximum relative duality gap of $1.3 \times 10^{-6}$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-real-data-path
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Benchmark for fitting the full regularization path on real data sets with
#|   varying path lengths. The plot shows the maximum relative duality gap
#|   across all solutions along the regularization path.
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("benchmark_path_real"))
```

Taken together, our benchmarks show that our method reaches a relative duality
gap of $10^{-7}$ first in 24 of the 27 single-solution settings and in eight of
the nine path settings. ADMM is faster in two single-solution settings, and
Newt-ALM is faster in one, while no solver reaches the threshold in the
remaining path setting. In contrast to @dupuis2024, who showed mixed results
when comparing their approximate homotopy method to the hybrid algorithm from
@larsson2023, we find a clearer advantage for the current hybrid implementation.
Possible explanations include the more stringent stopping criterion used by
@dupuis2024 (a duality gap of $10^{-10}$), the generally larger problems in our
benchmarks, and enhancements over the original hybrid implementation from
@larsson2023.

# Application to real-world data

To illustrate the practical utility of SLOPE, we applied it to a metabolomics
dataset from @Godlewski2023, comprising plasma measurements from glioma patients
and healthy controls. The dataset contains 165 samples (94 glioma cases and 71
controls), each with 138 metabolite features.

We first create the design matrix `x` and the response vector `y`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

x <- scale(glioma$x)
y <- glioma$y
```

We split the data into training and test sets before fitting the models. This
allows us to evaluate out-of-sample classification performance when
distinguishing glioma patients from healthy controls:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

set.seed(222)
train_index <- caret::createDataPartition(y, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
x_train <- x[train_index, ]
y_train <- y[train_index]
x_test <- x[-train_index, ]
y_test <- y[-train_index]
```

We then fit a SLOPE model with cross-validation on the training data to select
the regularization parameter. The function `cvSLOPE()` performs $K$-fold
cross-validation and optimizes over $\alpha$:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

slope_cv <- cvSLOPE(
  x_train,
  y_train,
  q = 0.1,
  family = "binomial",
  measure = "auc",
  n_folds = 10
)
alpha_cv <- slope_cv$optima$alpha
slope_model <- SLOPE(
  x_train,
  y_train,
  q = 0.1,
  family = "binomial",
  alpha = alpha_cv
)
```

Predicted probabilities for the test data can be obtained with the `predict()`
method:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

pred_prob <- predict(slope_model, x_test, type = "response")
```

For comparison, we fit a lasso model with `glmnet`, selecting its regularization
parameter by ten-fold cross-validation on the same training data. In this
example, SLOPE achieved an AUC of
`r sprintf("%.3f", paper_results$glioma$auc_slope)` on the test set, while the
lasso obtained `r sprintf("%.3f", paper_results$glioma$auc_lasso)`. Although the
lasso performed slightly better in terms of AUC, the fitted SLOPE model exhibits
the structure induced by the sorted $\ell_1$ penalty: it selected
`r paper_results$glioma$n_selected_slope` metabolites and organized them into
`r paper_results$glioma$n_clusters_slope` coefficient clusters. The lasso
selected `r paper_results$glioma$n_selected_lasso` metabolites without grouping
them.

One of the features of the R implementation is the ability to visualize the
clustering of coefficients with the `plotClusters()` function.[^cluster-plot] We
fit a regularization path to the training data and mark the step corresponding
to the value of $\alpha$ selected by cross-validation. The plot highlights
groups of variables with coefficients of the same magnitude (up to sign):

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

slope_model_path <- SLOPE(
  x_train,
  y_train,
  q = 0.1,
  patterns = TRUE,
  family = "binomial"
)
selected_step <- which.min(abs(slope_model_path$alpha - alpha_cv))
plotClusters(slope_model_path, include_zeroes = FALSE)
abline(
  v = (selected_step - 1) / (length(slope_model_path$alpha) - 1),
  col = "firebrick",
  lty = 2,
  lwd = 1.5
)
mtext(sprintf("Selected step %d", selected_step), side = 3, line = 0.5)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-real-data-clusters
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Cluster structure along the SLOPE regularization path for the training
#|   data. Variables are grouped by effect size, with colors indicating distinct
#|   clusters. The marked step corresponds to the regularization parameter
#|   selected by cross-validation.
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("glioma-clusters"))
```

This produces a cluster map of selected metabolites, revealing the grouping
behavior of SLOPE (@fig-real-data-clusters). At the value of $\alpha$ selected
by cross-validation, one cluster comprises *lysine*, *phenylalanine*, and PC aa
C34:1, while another comprises *alanine* and *kynurenine*. The latter is a known
glioma biomarker [@du2020both], and both *phenylalanine* and *lysine* have been
associated with glioma-related metabolic changes
[@koslinski2023comparative; @srivastava2025amino]. The largest cluster contains
*asparagine*, *methionine*, PC ae C42:5, and SM C18:0. These groupings
illustrate how SLOPE can select variables jointly and assign them coefficients
with the same magnitude (up to sign).

Overall, this example demonstrates how the package can be applied in practice.
Beyond predictive performance, its functionality, such as cross-validation,
prediction, and cluster visualization, makes it a useful tool for
high-dimensional biomedical data analysis, where interpretability and feature
selection are essential.

[^cluster-plot]: This functionality is specific to the R package.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

SLOPE is an appealing model for high-dimensional regression problems that is
able to recover sparsity and ordering patterns in the solution, which sets it
apart from similar models such as the lasso and elastic net. Unlike these models
however, SLOPE represents a more challenging optimization problem due to the
penalty term's inseparability.

Despite the complexity of the problem, we have here presented a collection of
packages (in R, Python, Julia, and C++) that offer efficient and feature-rich
implementations of SLOPE. We hope that this endeavor will make SLOPE accessible
to a wider audience. Other implementations include **skglm** and the specialized
approximate path method **SolutionPath**; our suite instead provides a common
implementation and feature set across four programming languages.

Our benchmarks show that the software generally performs strongly compared with
the other algorithms and implementations considered here, both for fitting the
full regularization path and for a single solution on real and simulated data.

Our results support the effectiveness of the hybrid algorithm approach, with
performance improvements over @larsson2023 following the addition of screening
rules and other algorithmic enhancements. The method reaches the reported
accuracy threshold first in most of the settings considered here, including
eight of the nine path-fitting settings, while other solvers are faster in three
single-solution settings. No solver reaches the threshold in the remaining
path-fitting setting.

Although our packages are full-fledged implementations of SLOPE, there are still
some features that are missing and feature coverage is generally not on par with
that of, for instance, **glmnet** for elastic net. For instance, we do not yet
support observation weights or the full suite of loss functions from the family
of generalized linear models. On the other hand, we *do* support out-of-memory
storage and much more granular normalization options, which are not supported in
**glmnet**. We also do not yet support the group sorted $\ell_1$ norm, which
would allow for an alternative penalization scheme for multivariate response
problems. In addition, several possible improvements to the hybrid method could
be considered, such as accelerated and parallelized coordinate steps. We leave
these possibilities to future work but want to stress that our packages are
modular and have been designed with extensibility in mind, which we hope will
facilitate the addition of new features in the future. Because all of the
packages rely on the same C++ library, contributions will also propagate
directly to the higher-level packages in R, Julia, and Python.

We hope that our packages will be useful for researchers and practitioners alike
and that the design of our software suite might inspire others to more closely
couple the available features of R, Python, and Julia, and avoid redundant
implementations of the same algorithms in each language.

# Data and code availability {#data-and-code-availability .unnumbered}

The source code for the software packages is available from the repositories
listed in @tbl-slope-packages. The code for the examples, analyses, and figures,
together with the benchmark configurations, results, and pinned software
environment, is available at
[`github.com/jolars/slope-package-paper`](https://github.com/jolars/slope-package-paper).
The single-solution and path benchmark repositories are
[`github.com/benchopt/benchmark_slope`](https://github.com/benchopt/benchmark_slope)
and
[`github.com/jolars/benchmark_slope_path`](https://github.com/jolars/benchmark_slope_path),
respectively.

The benchmark repositories contain code to generate the simulated data and
download the real datasets. `BRCA1`, `Koussounadis2014`, and `Rhee2006` are
available from Patrick Breheny's collection at
[`github.com/IowaBiostat/data-sets`](https://github.com/IowaBiostat/data-sets);
`Real-Sim`, `RCV1`, and `YearPredictionMSD` are available from the LIBSVM data
collection of @chang2016. The diabetes data are included in the paper repository
as `data/diabetes.csv`, and the glioma data from @Godlewski2023 are distributed
as `glioma` in the R package **SLOPE**. All data used in this study are publicly
available without registration.

# Examples in Julia, Python, and C++ {#sec-examples-julia-python .appendix}

In this section, we provide Python, Julia, and C++ equivalents of the R examples
from @sec-first-steps. As in the R case, some of the plotting code has been
simplified for clarity. Please refer to the code repository for the full code.

## Julia

We begin by loading the necessary packages.

```julia
using SLOPE
using CSV
using ProjectRoot
using DataFrames
using Statistics
using Random
using Plots
```

Next, we load the diabetes data set, which we have made available as a CSV file
in the `data` directory of the repository. As before, we standardize the
features to have mean zero and unit variance.

```julia
file = @projectroot "data/diabetes.csv"
df = CSV.read(file, DataFrame)
x = Matrix(df[:, 2:end])
y = df[:, 1]

x_means = mean(x, dims = 1)
x_std = std(x, dims = 1)
x = (x .- x_means) ./ x_std
```

We then fit SLOPE and lasso models to the data. Note that the `lambda` argument
is actually the symbol $\lambda$ in the Julia package, so this code will not
work if you write `lambda = "lasso"`.

```julia
fit_lasso = slope(x, y, λ = :lasso)
fit_slope = slope(x, y, λ = :bh)
```

Just like the R package, the Julia package supports plotting the solution paths
directly. Here, we create a combined plot showing both the lasso and SLOPE paths
side by side (@fig-diabetes-julia).

```julia
plot(
    plot(fit_lasso),
    plot(fit_slope),
    layout = (1, 2),
    size = (400, 200),
    title = ["Lasso" "SLOPE"],
)
```
```{r}
#| label: fig-diabetes-julia
#| fig-pos: H
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   SLOPE and lasso paths on the diabetes data set. Note that the $x$ axis is
#|   reversed.
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("diabetes-slope-lasso-julia"))
```

To perform cross-validation, we use the `slopecv` function, which also features
a dedicated `plot` method[^11].

```julia
Random.seed!(48)
fit_cv = slopecv(x, y)
pcv = plot(fit_cv)
```

The result is shown in @fig-cv-julia.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cv-julia
#| fig-pos: H
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Mean-squared error (MSE) from cross-validation over $\alpha$, with $q =
#|   0.1$, for SLOPE fit to the diabetes data set. The ribbon represents a 95%
#|   confidence interval.
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("slope-cv-julia"))
```

## Python

We begin by loading the necessary packages.

```python
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sortedl1 import Slope
```

Next, we load the diabetes data set from **scikit-learn** and standardize the
features to have mean zero and unit variance.

```python
x, y = load_diabetes(return_X_y=True)
scaler = StandardScaler()
x = scaler.fit_transform(x)
```

We then create SLOPE models with lasso and BH penalty sequences.

```python
model_lasso = Slope(lambda_type="lasso")
model_slope = Slope(lambda_type="bh", q=0.4)
```

We fit the models to the data using the `path` method.

```python
fit_lasso = model_lasso.path(x, y)
fit_slope = model_slope.path(x, y)
```

Just like the R and Julia packages, the Python package supports plotting the
solution paths. The result is shown in @fig-diabetes-python.

```python
fit_lasso.plot()
plt.title("Lasso")
plt.show()

fit_slope.plot()
plt.title("SLOPE")
plt.show()
```
::: {#fig-diabetes-python layout-ncol=2 fig-pos="H"}
```{r}
#| label: plot-diabetes-python
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("diabetes-slope-python"))
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-diabetes-python-lasso
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(paper_figure("diabetes-lasso-python"))
```

SLOPE and lasso paths on the diabetes data set. Note that the $x$ axis is
reversed.
:::

To perform cross-validation, we use the `cv` method.

```python
fit_cv = model_slope.cv(x, y, q=[0.1, 0.2])
fit_cv.plot()
```

# Duality gap and convergence criteria {#sec-convergence-criteria-details .appendix}

For clarity, we first use the scalar-response notation from @sec-math-details;
the multinomial extension follows below. We absorb $\alpha$ into $\lambda$,
introduce the linear predictors $\eta_i$, and write the primal problem in
constrained form:
$$
  \begin{aligned}
    \mathop{\mathrm{minimize}}_{\beta_0 \in \mathbb{R},\,\beta \in \mathbb{R}^p,\,\eta \in \mathbb{R}^n} \quad & \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f(\eta_i, y_i) + J_\lambda(\beta)  \\
    \text{subject to} \quad                                                                                    & \eta_i = \beta_0 + x_i^\top \beta, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n.
  \end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-primal-constrained}

Using multipliers $\delta_i/n$ gives the Lagrangian
$$
  L(\beta_0, \beta, \eta, \delta)
  = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ f(\eta_i, y_i) - \delta_i(\eta_i - x_i^\top\beta - \beta_0) \right]
    + J_\lambda(\beta).
$$

Let $f_i^*$ denote the Fenchel conjugate of $f_i(\eta) = f(\eta,y_i)$.
Minimizing over $\eta$ gives
$$
  \inf_{\eta_i}\{f_i(\eta_i) - \delta_i\eta_i\} = -f_i^*(\delta_i).
$$

The terms involving $\beta$ give
$$
  \inf_\beta \left\{ J_\lambda(\beta) + \left( \frac{X^\top\delta}{n} \right)^\top\beta \right\}
  = -J_\lambda^*\left( -\frac{X^\top\delta}{n} \right).
$$

Here, the Fenchel conjugate of the sorted $\ell_1$ norm is the indicator of its
dual-norm unit ball:
$$
  J_\lambda^*(z) = \begin{cases}
                     0      & \text{if } \lVert z \rVert_{*,\lambda} \leq 1, \\
                     \infty & \text{otherwise},
                   \end{cases}
$$
where the sorted $\ell_1$ dual norm is [@negrinho2014]
$$
  \lVert z \rVert_{*,\lambda}
  = \max_{j=1,2,\dots,p} \left\{ \frac{\sum_{k=1}^j|z_{(k)}|}{\sum_{k=1}^j\lambda_k} \right\}.
$$ {#eq-slope-dual-norm}

Finally, minimizing over the unpenalized intercept is finite only when
$\boldsymbol{1}^\top\delta = 0$. The dual problem is therefore
$$
  D(\delta) = \begin{cases}
                -\dfrac{1}{n}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n f_i^*(\delta_i) & \text{if } \left\lVert -\dfrac{X^\top\delta}{n} \right\rVert_{*,\lambda} \leq 1,\; \boldsymbol{1}^\top\delta = 0, \\
                -\infty                                                & \text{otherwise}.
              \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-slope-dual}
As usual, $f_i^*(\delta_i) = \infty$ outside its domain, so domain feasibility
is implicit in @eq-slope-dual. If the model has no intercept, the condition
$\boldsymbol{1}^\top\delta = 0$ is omitted.

For the canonical generalized linear models considered here, let
$q_i = y_i + \delta_i$. The conjugate domain requires $q_i$ to belong to the
mean-parameter domain $\mathcal{M}$. This domain is $\mathbb{R}$ for the
Gaussian model, $[0,1]$ for the binomial model, $[0,\infty)$ for the Poisson
model, and
$$
  \mathcal{M}
  = \left\{ q \in \mathbb{R}^{m-1}: q_k \geq 0,\; \sum_{k=1}^{m-1}q_k \leq 1 \right\}
$$
for the non-redundant multinomial model. In the multinomial case, we define the
reference-class mean as $q_{im} = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{m-1}q_{ik}$. Using the
convention $0\log 0 = 0$, the loss-specific terms in @eq-slope-dual are
$$
  -f_i^*(\delta_i) = \begin{cases}
                       -y_i\delta_i - \frac{1}{2}\delta_i^2         & \text{Gaussian},    \\
                       -q_i\log q_i - (1 - q_i)\log(1 - q_i)        & \text{binomial},    \\
                       q_i(1 - \log q_i)                            & \text{Poisson},     \\
                       -\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^m q_{ik}\log q_{ik} & \text{multinomial}.
                     \end{cases}
$$
For example, the Gaussian dual objective is
$$
  D(\delta) = \frac{\lVert y\rVert_2^2 - \lVert y + \delta\rVert_2^2}{2n}
$$
at a feasible point.

The generalized residual $r_i = g^{-1}(\beta_0 + x_i^\top\beta) - y_i$ is a
natural dual candidate: at the optimum, the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker conditions
include
$$
  \boldsymbol{0} \in \frac{X^\top r}{n} + \partial J_\lambda(\beta),
  \qquad
  \boldsymbol{1}^\top r = 0.
$$

Away from the optimum, however, centering $r$ is safe only for the Gaussian
model. For the other models, centering can move $y_i + r_i$ outside
$\mathcal{M}$. We instead construct a zero-sum point that remains in the
conjugate domain. Let
$$
  c_i = r_i - \bar r, \qquad a_i = \bar y - y_i,
$$
and define
$$
  t_{\max}
  = \max\left\{ t \in[0,1] : y_i + a_i + t(c_i - a_i) \in \mathcal{M} \text{ for every }i \right\}.
$$

Then
$$
  \widetilde\delta_i = a_i + t_{\max}(c_i - a_i)
$$
satisfies both $\boldsymbol{1}^\top\widetilde\delta = 0$ and
$y_i + \widetilde\delta_i \in \mathcal{M}$. The set defining $t_{\max}$ is
nonempty because $t = 0$ gives $y_i + a_i = \bar y \in \mathcal{M}$. For a model
without an intercept, we instead take $\widetilde\delta = r$, which is already
in the conjugate domain.

It remains to enforce the sorted $\ell_1$ dual constraint. Set
$$
  \rho
  = \max\left\{ 1, \left\lVert -\frac{X^\top\widetilde\delta}{n} \right\rVert_{*,\lambda} \right\},
  \qquad
  \delta = \frac{\widetilde\delta}{\rho}.
$$

This scaling preserves every other constraint. In particular,
$$
  y_i + \delta_i = \left( 1 - \frac{1}{\rho} \right)y_i
                   + \frac{1}{\rho}(y_i + \widetilde\delta_i) \in \mathcal{M}
$$
by convexity of $\mathcal{M}$. For binomial and Poisson models, our
implementation obtains a tighter initial point by conditionally adjusting the
intercept so that the residuals sum to zero. It uses the domain-preserving
construction above as a numerical repair and as the primary construction for the
multinomial model. For multinomial regression, the intercept condition holds
componentwise across the nonreference classes, whereas domain feasibility is
imposed jointly on each row through the simplex $\mathcal{M}$. The regularizer
constraint is also joint: the matrix $X^\top\widetilde\delta/n$ is vectorized
before evaluating the sorted $\ell_1$ dual norm.

At this feasible point, the duality gap
$$
  P(\beta_0,\beta) - D(\delta)
$$
is nonnegative and bounds the primal suboptimality. We stop when the relative
duality gap satisfies
$$
  P(\beta_0,\beta) - D(\delta) \leq \varepsilon\lvert P(\beta_0,\beta)\rvert,
$$
where $\varepsilon > 0$ is the user-defined tolerance level. The availability of
the duality gap would also allow us to employ duality-gap based safe screening
rules [@fercoq2015] and working set strategies derived from
these [@massias2018], which could furthermore be used to enhance our strategy
with look-ahead screening rules [@larsson2021a]. However, as noted in
@larsson2022d, the marginal improvement of using duality-based screening
strategies is minor, so we have opted not to implement these in our packages.

# Solver details {#sec-solver-details .appendix}

sortedl1

:   The python package of our implementation of the hybrid proximal
    gradient/coordinate descent algorithm described in this work and
    @larsson2023. We use the randomized version of the coordinate descent
    updates.

Anderson PGD

:   The proximal gradient descent (PGD) algorithm with Anderson acceleration,
    which is a method for accelerating the convergence of fixed-point
    iterations [@anderson1965; @zhang2020].

BB PGD

:   PGD with Barzilai--Borwein [@barzilai1988] step sizes.

FISTA

:   Fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding [@beck2009], which accelerates
    ISTA [@wright2009].

Safe PGD

:   FISTA with acceleration using safe screening rules [@elvira2023].

ADMM

:   The alternating direction method of multipliers [@glowinski1975; @boyd2010],
    which is a popular algorithm for solving convex optimization problems with
    constraints. In our experiments, we have used $\rho = 100$ as a step size
    based on the results from @larsson2023. We considered using the heuristic
    $\rho$ selection method from @boyd2010, but have avoided doing so since it,
    as shown by @larsson2023, may lead to erratic convergence behavior in
    practice. We use `lsqr()` from **SciPy** [@virtanen2020] to solve the linear
    system if $\min\{n, p\} > 1,000$ and otherwise solve the linear system as
    suggested by @boyd2010.

Newt-ALM

:   A semi-smooth Newton-based method [@luo2019]. Our implementation of this
    method is based on that from @larsson2023, but improved with better
    heuristics for selecting the inner solver, improved conjugate gradient
    solver, and a bug fix for the Woodbury-based solver. For the conjugate
    gradient solver, we use `cg()` from **SciPy** [@virtanen2020].

skglm

:   Another implementation of FISTA from the **skglm** package [@bertrand2022].

tick

:   FISTA from the **tick** package [@bacry2018], using its SLOPE proximal
    operator. We use a fixed step size equal to the inverse of the average
    sample Lipschitz constant, which supports both dense and sparse designs.

SolutionPath

:   An approximate homotopy method by @dupuis2024, which is similar to the lars
    algorithm for the lasso [@efron2004].

[^1]: The lasso is attained by taking a constant $\lambda$.

[^2]: OSCAR is attained by setting $\lambda$ to be a linear sequence, where
    $\lambda_j = \theta_1 + \theta_2(p - j)$ with
    $\theta_1, \theta_2 \geq 0$ [@figueiredo2014].

[^3]: At an average $p \log p$ rate, due to the limiting sorting operation.

[^4]: SLOPE is sometimes used only as the procedure that uses quadratic loss,
    but here we adopt a more general terminology and let SLOPE be defined for
    any loss function.

[^5]: The non-redundant formulation requires a $\lambda$ sequence of length
    $(m - 1)p$. It would therefore not reduce to the binary formulation if we
    instead used $m$ coefficient vectors.

[^6]: As opposed to the lasso, which at most allows $n$ non-zero *coefficients*.

[^7]: Note that the actual code for the plotting examples here is slightly more
    complex to allow for better control over the aesthetics.

[^8]: Note that this paper refers to the relaxed SLOPE as the "debiased" SLOPE.
    Here, we prefer the term "relaxed"' to stay closer to the nomenclature from
    the lasso literature and avoid confusion with the debiased
    lasso [@geer2014], which represents a different approach.

[^9]: The R package **SLOPE** is also included, but we have omitted it from the
    benchmark here since it is essentially equivalent to the Python package
    **sortedl1**.

[^11]: Note that our package only provides a recipe for the **Plots.jl**
    package, and does not depend on it directly. Users need to load the
    **Plots.jl** package (as we do here) to have access to these plotting
    methods.

[^12]: This is included in the supplementary material as well.
